link.title: Mastering Graph ML: Traditional Approaches to Generating Graphs

entry.content:
From social networks to molecular structures, how do we “fake” the complexity of real-world graphs? Discover the foundational math and logic behind the traditional models that first taught us how to generate graphs.

So far in this series, we’ve focused on graph representation learning, but there is also a complementary task that deserves our attention: graph generation. The goal here is to create realistic graph structures. This can be viewed as the “mirror” problem of graph representation learning, whereas representation learning maps a graph to a vector space, graph generation maps a distribution or a latent code back into a graph

Generating graphs isn’t inherently difficult. After all, it is trivial to build a fully-connected graph or a random one. However, these structures are rarely useful because real-world graphs possess specific, “desirable” properties. The true challenge lies in duplicating these intricate properties to create synthetic graphs that are indistinguishable from the real ones.

Traditional approaches to graph generation generally involve specifying a generative process, which defines how the edges in a graph are created. In general, this process boils down to sampling each potential edge based on a specified probability or likelihood

Erdös-Renyi Approach

The simplest and most well-known generative model of graphs is the Erdös-Renyi (ER) model. In this framework, we define the likelihood of an edge occurring between any pair of nodes as

where 0<p<1 is the parameter controlling the density of the graph. Essentially, every possible edge in the graph has the same independent probability of existing.

Let’s see how it works in practice. Suppose we start with a set of 5 nodes.

We focus on the first node and sample its potential edges with the other nodes according to the likelihood of an edge. In this example, we will use p=0.3 arbitrarily.

We then repeat this process for all other nodes in the graph.

Finally, the output of the ER model is an adjacency matrix that represents the structure of the generated graph.

Note that while I’ve explained the ER model sequentially to illustrate the logic, in practice, we can sample the entire adjacency matrix at once. For directed graphs, we sample every entry; for undirected graphs, we only sample the upper (or lower) triangle to ensure symmetry.

The downside of this simple model is that it rarely generates realistic graphs. Since all edges are sampled uniformly and independently, the model fails to produce the community structures often observed in social networks or biological systems.

Stochastic Block Models

Stochastic Block Models (SBMs) are one of these approaches that aim to improve upon the ER model to capture real-world graph properties. With the SBM method, the goal is to generate graphs that present community structures, similar to those found in real-world social or biological networks.

Let’s briefly explain how it works. SBMs start by assigning nodes to a block Cᵢ (corresponding to a community) by sampling from a given categorical distribution (p₁, …, pₖ). Then, for every pair of nodes u in community Cᵢ and v in community Cⱼ, SBMs sample an edge according to

where C is a connectivity matrix describing the likelihood of an edge between nodes of different communities.

To make it clearer, let’s illustrate this with a simple example. Suppose we have 5 nodes, and we start by assigning these nodes to 3 possible communities as follows

Then, we specify a matrix that describes how these communities interact with each other — essentially a matrix that translates the likelihood of an edge appearing between nodes based on their group membership.

Finally, just like with the ER model, we sample edges according to a probability. The key difference is that in the ER model, the probability is constant for all pairs of nodes, whereas in SBMs, the probability depends on the communities of the nodes. For example, let’s look at a red node in the graph.

The previous figure illustrates that the bottom red node has a probability of 0.8 to have an edge with each yellow node individually and of 0.2 to have an edge with the only green node. Here, the fact that 0 is the first diagonal element translates to the fact that nodes from the red community can never be linked together. You can imagine particles with the same electric charge that are attracted to opposite charges but repulsed by particles of the same charge.

Sampling according to these probabilities can yield a structure like this

We then repeat this operation for all other nodes.

In summary, SBMs take the community assignment probabilities and a connectivity matrix as input, and output a graph with a specific community structure.

In this simple example, the community structures might not be visually obvious because the graph has so few nodes. However, the power of SBMs to create distinct “clusters” is best illustrated when the number of nodes is increased significantly.

Preferential Attachment

Another characteristic of real-world graphs that one might want to replicate is the power law that node degree follows. First, let’s illustrate what this means in social networks. For instance, on Instagram, the average number of followers is 264, and only a few celebrities have more than 10 million followers. Mathematically, the power law is described by

The preferential attachment (PA) model attempts to capture the characteristics of real-world degree distributions using a simple iterative generative process.

The general idea of the previous formula is: the more connections a node already has, the more likely it is to get the next one. Let’s work through this process to create a simple 5-node graph. Suppose we chose m₀=3 and start with a fully connected graph with 3 nodes.

We need to add iteratively 2 nodes to this graph. So, let’s first add one

and sample the red nodes’ edges according to the formula given above.

To finish the graph generation, we add the last node

and sample its edges according to the same formula as before.

Again, in this simple example, the node degree power law distribution might not be visually obvious because the graph has so few nodes. However, the power of the PA model to create a node degree power law distribution is best illustrated when the number of nodes is increased significantly.

Graph Generation and Evaluation

To evaluate the quality of the generated graphs, the current practice is to analyze different statistics of the generated graphs and to compare the distribution of statistics for the generated graphs to a test set.
For instance, we can compute the distance between the statistic’s distribution on the test graph and the generated graph using a distributional measure, such as the total variation (TV) distance.

More clearly, the TV distance measures the overlap between two probability distributions. For example, if one looks at the node degree, calculating the TV distance can be thought of as looking at every possible value (e.g., nodes with degree 5), finding the difference in how often that value appears in the real vs. synthetic datasets, and taking the maximum of these differences. Hence, a TV distance of 0 means the distributions are identical, and a TV distance of 1 means they have nothing in common.

Applications and Limits

The first useful application of these generative models is that they can be used for synthetic graphs for benchmarking and analysis tasks. In a statistical sense, they provide us with a null models that we can use as reference points for our understanding of real-world graphs.

However, these approaches come with three main disadvantages:

  • These approaches can generate graphs, but they cannot learn a generative model from data; therefore, we need prior knowledge of the graphs we want to generate, which may not be available for some tasks.
  • Also, real graphs aren’t just dots and lines; nodes have features, and traditional models struggle to generate these attributes alongside the structure.
  • Finally, real-world graphs often exhibit “hierarchical” structures (communities within communities), and traditional approaches are usually too flat to capture them.

In other words, traditional models like Erdös-Renyi, Stochastic Block Models, or Preferential Attachment are quite useful in their simplicity, but they require us to guess beforehand the underlying rules of a network before we can simulate it. In real world scenarii, graphs are messy, often multi-layered, and, in some cases, massive, which makes guessing the underlying rules really hard. This is where Deep Generative Methods come in handy, as we’ll later see in another article.

Conclusions

In this article, we unpacked the most frequently used traditional methods for generating graphs: Erdös-Renyi, Stochastic Block Models, and Preferential Attachment, and saw how they try to capture some characteristics of real-world graphs. We then try to show how to evaluate them before showing their applications and limits

What’s coming next? Now that we’ve introduced traditional approaches to graph generation and discussed their limitations. We’ll cover in the next article deep generative methods for graph generation and how they deal with some of the disadvantages of traditional graph generation methods.

This article is part of a series that will help you understand how graph machine learning works:

  1. Introduction to Graph Data
  2. Traditional Approaches to Machine Learning on Graphs
    -     Node, Edge, and Graph Statistics
    -     Graph Spectral Clustering
    -     Node Embeddings
  3. Deep Learning Methods
    -     Graph Neural Networks and the Message Passing Framework
    -     Improving Graph Neural Networks
  4. Generating Graphs
    -     Traditional Approaches to Generating Graphs
    - Deep Generative Methods
  5. Theoretical Motivations (Bonus)
    - GNNs and Graph Convolutions
    - GNNs and Probabilistic Graphical Models
    - GNNs and Graph Isomorphisms

Presentation of the Series “Mastering Graph ML”

Graph Machine Learning receives little attention compared to other fields of machine learning, like Natural Language Modeling with LLMs, Reinforcement Learning with RL from human feedback, or Computer Vision with Diffusion models used in image generation. However, at the time of writing, the latest improvements in Gemini (Google LLM) were about refining the computational graph of the attention mechanism. In my opinion, this example illustrates the importance of learning Graph Machine Learning, and this series of articles is my effort to highlight it.

A great part of what is going to be written in this series is inspired by a wonderful book on graph machine learning (perhaps the best you can find), Graph Representation Learning [1]. Other parts will come from papers or resources I read during my PhD.

entry.title: Mastering Graph ML: Improving GNNs
entry.content:
Stop stacking GNN layers and hoping for the best — oversmoothing, oversquashing, and under-reaching are probably sabotaging your model long before you hit “train.”

Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated strong performance on various graph-related tasks, their message-passing scheme has limitations and drawbacks. These issues can be tackled with several techniques to enhance GNNs. Before delving deeper into this method, I’ll explain the three most common problems arising when building GNNs: oversmoothing, oversquashing, and under-reaching.

Oversmoothing, oversquashing, and under-reaching

At each GNN layer, the message-passing scheme aggregates the features of each node’s neighbors and inputs them into a non-linear activation function. This way, we’re able to update a node’s representation based on the graph signal and the graph structure.

However, when stacking many GNN layers (a common practice in many other deep learning architectures), node representations become increasingly similar, eventually “smoothing out” all distinctions across the graph.

Why does this happen? In GNNs, with each additional layer, information diffuses one more hop out. Indeed, at the first layer, a node receives information from its neighbors via the aggregation scheme. Then, at the second layer, since its neighbors received their neighbors’ information at the first layer, a node receives the information of its 2-hop neighborhood (i.e., its neighbors’ neighbors). After many layers, every node’s embedding converges toward the stationary distribution of this diffusion process, washing away the local structures and the graph signal.

In practice, oversmoothing constraints GNNs to have 5 layers or fewer.

Another problem related to GNN layer information aggregation is oversquashing. Oversquashing occurs when long-range signals from distant nodes in the graph are “squashed” into fixed-dimensional embeddings, rendering it impossible to propagate complex information across multiple hops.

To explain how it happens in detail, as you add layers, the number of source nodes grows exponentially, but you still compress their information into a vector of fixed size. This causes an information bottleneck where distinctions are lost. With oversquashing, the deeper the receptive field (the number of information source nodes), the worse the squashing.

Let’s illustrate this with an example. Let’s say we’re trying to update the red node representation on the following graph:

When applying the first GNN layer, the message-passing scheme aggregates the neighbors’ information into a vector of size n.

Then, the second layer aggregates the neighbors’ neighbors and the neighbors’ information into a vector whose size is still n, even though the number of information source nodes is drastically higher.

Even though adding a third layer to the following graph only adds two information source nodes compared to the second layer. In practice, adding a layer multiplies the number of source nodes by the average degree in the graph.

To sum up, the number of information source nodes after K layers is the average degree to the power of K. All this information is stored in a vector of constant size, which leads to the loss of information because the vector does not have enough numbers to account for the distinction in information from all source nodes.

A quick solution that tackles both oversmoothing and oversquashing is to limit the number of layers in GNNs. Even though this solution works well, it also comes with the problem of under-reaching. Under-reaching stems from the fact that shallow GNNs (GNNs with few layers) can only aggregate information from nodes within their limited number of hops, hence failing to capture dependencies from farther nodes.

Let’s illustrate with the previous graph example.

At the first layer, the red node receives information from its neighbors

Then, it receives information from its neighbors and their neighbors.

Even with this simple graph example, a GNN with only two layers failed to capture dependencies between the red node and the nodes that remained white in the previous image.

Knowing these three problem behaviors of GNNs is crucial in designing powerful graph models. Indeed, some of these behaviors can be harmless depending on the task at hand.

For instance, oversmoothing can be harmless in graph classification where GNNs are used to generate graph embeddings. In that case, any node representation (which will be the same for all nodes) can be used as a graph embedding. However, oversmoothing hurts tasks that rely on preserving differences between nodes, such as node classification in heterophilic graphs.

Tricks against oversmoothing

Oversmoothing seems to arise in GNNs because the message-passing scheme that we’ve described before depends too strongly on the incoming message aggregated from the neighbors at the expense of the node representations from the previous layer.

A natural way to tackle this issue is to induce a stronger bias on the node representation from the previous layer during the message-passing scheme. One way to do this is to use skip-connections, which try to preserve information from the previous node representation during the message-passing scheme.

There are several options to make skip connections. The simplest one is to concatenate the previous node representation with the output of the non-linear activation.

In addition to concatenation skip-connections, a solution would be to assign weights to the previous node representation and the output of the non-linear activation. This mechanism would allow the model to freely learn the weights and to give more importance to whether the previous node representation or the output of the non-linear activation, depending on the task.

A complementary approach to enhance the quality of the final node representations is to utilize the representations from each message-passing layer, rather than relying solely on the output of the final layer. This is known as jumping knowledge. In the jumping knowledge approach, the representations from each message-passing layer are concatenated and input into an arbitrary differentiable function.

Leverage more data

Up to this point, our discussion of GNNs and neural message passing has focused on simple graphs. However, many real-world applications involve graphs that are multi-relational or heterogeneous, such as knowledge graphs. In this section, we explore the most widely used approach designed to handle this type of data.

As a reminder, a multi-relational or heterogeneous graph is a graph where two nodes can be linked by different types of edges. If you need to refresh your memory on the different types of graphs, I recommend reading the first article in the series, Mastering Graph ML: Introduction to graph data.

The simplest way to learn on this type of data is to learn considering each edge type independently, using the methods we’ve seen on simple graphs, and to concatenate the results for each edge type.

So, let’s start with the yellow edge type. The message passing operation acts as if the graph were only composed of the three nodes connected by yellow edges.

Then, we repeat the same operation for the green edge type and add it to the message passing.

Finally, the global message passing is given by adding the message passing on the red edge type.

This simple yet powerful method to deal with multi-relational graphs is known as the Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). It is summarized by the following equation,

where R represents the different edge types and f_n is a node normalisation function that can depend on both the neighborhood of the node u as well as the neighbor V being aggregated over.

So far, we have primarily focused on the most common form of GNN message passing, which primarily operates at the node level. However, the message passing framework for GNNs can be extended to incorporate edge-level and graph-level information at each step of the process. This approach is known as Generalised Message Passing.

First, let’s remember that to encode more information in our graph than just with node features, we can also add edge features and even a graph feature.

The Generalised Message Passing approach sequentially updates the edges, nodes, and graph representation. It starts by updating the edge representations based on their previous representations, the previous representations of the nodes that composed the edges, and the previous representation of the graph.

Then, the approach updates the nodes’ representation by a modified version of the message passing scheme. Instead of using the representation of a node’s neighbors to update its representation, it uses the representation of the adjacent edges in the message passing.

Finally, the updated representations of nodes and edges are used to update the graph representation in the final step of the generalised message passing.

We can then summarize the Generalised Message Passing as the following sequential approach

GNNs limitations

Previously, we have focused on the theoretical limits of GNNs without also taking into account the practical limits of GNNs. Amongst these limits, we can identify 3 main problems: redundant computations, the memory footprint of GNNs, and the uselessness of pre-training.

Redundant computations appear when using node-level message passing equations. Implementing a GNN directly based on these equations can lead to computational inefficiencies. For instance, if multiple nodes share common neighbors, performing message passing operations independently for each node may result in repeated and unnecessary calculations.

To deal with this issue, the most efficient approach to reduce the number of mathematical operations required for message passing is to implement the GNN equations at the graph level.

However, in some cases, as in the Generalised Message Passing, the message passing mechanism is too complex to be reduced to a graph-level equation, leading to computational inefficiencies in the implementation of these methods.

Another important aspect to keep in mind when dealing with GNNs is their memory footprint as the number of nodes and edges grows larger. To reduce the memory usage of a GNN and enable mini-batch training, message passing can be performed on a subset of nodes. Mathematically, this involves applying the node-level GNN equations to a selected subset of nodes in the graph for each batch. By carefully designing the implementation, redundant computations can be avoided, ensuring that the embedding for each node in the batch is computed at most once during model execution.

The challenge with this approach lies in the fact that running message passing on only a subset of nodes in a graph can result in information loss because removing a node also eliminates its edges, effectively altering the adjacency matrix. Additionally, randomly selecting a subset of nodes does not ensure the resulting graph will remain connected, and therefore, using a random subset of nodes for each mini-batch can significantly degrade model performance.

Hamilton et al. [4] proposed a strategy to address this issue by sub-sampling node neighborhoods. The method involves first selecting a set of target nodes for a batch and then recursively sampling their neighbors to preserve the graph’s connectivity. To prevent excessive node sampling within a batch, they suggest sub-sampling each node’s neighbors using a fixed sample size, which enhances the efficiency of batched tensor operations. For more detailed explanations of how GraphSAGE works, I recommend reading another article in the series, Mastering Graph ML: GNNs and the message-passing framework.

The last main limitation of GNNs in practice is pre-training. In the last few years, pre-training has become a standard component of deep learning pipelines, especially with LLMs. Hence, it is natural to consider whether pre-training with neighborhood reconstruction objectives could improve performance on downstream classification tasks for GNNs.

Most unsupervised GNN pre-training methods aim either to maximize mutual information across different representation levels or to distinguish real node–embedding pairs from corrupted ones. Surprisingly, these approaches have shown limited effectiveness for GNNs. Veličković et al. [2], for instance, reported that randomly initialized GNNs perform on par with models pre-trained using neighborhood reconstruction losses.

A common explanation is that message passing already embeds substantial neighborhood information: nodes that are close in the graph naturally receive similar representations, making explicit neighborhood reconstruction somewhat redundant. Despite this, developing more effective GNN pre-training methods remains an active and open research direction.

Conclusions

In this article, we unpacked the core pathologies of GNNs — oversmoothing, oversquashing, and under-reaching — and saw how they fundamentally constrain depth and expressivity along with the often-overlooked computational and practical limits of GNNs. We then walked through practical design tricks to make GNNs more robust and informative. Taken together, these ideas provide a roadmap for using today’s GNNs more effectively.

What’s coming next? Now that we have introduced GNNs and the issues they present, we can discuss the graphs used to evaluate them. Most of the time, these graphs originate from real-world datasets; however, depending on the task at hand, it may be useful to generate synthetic graphs instead. Generating graphs will be the focus of the next two articles.

This article is part of a series that will help you understand how graph machine learning works:

  1. Introduction to Graph Data
  2. Traditional Approaches to Machine Learning on Graphs
    -     Node, Edge, and Graph Statistics
    -     Graph Spectral Clustering
    -     Node Embeddings
  3. Deep Learning Methods
    -     Graph Neural Networks and the Message Passing Framework
    -     Improving Graph Neural Networks (this post)
  4. Generating Graphs
    - Traditional Approaches to Generating Graphs
    - Deep Generative Methods
  5. Theoretical Motivations (Bonus)
    - GNNs and Graph Convolutions
    - GNNs and Probabilistic Graphical Models
    - GNNs and Graph Isomorphisms

Presentation of the Series “Mastering Graph ML”

Graph Machine Learning receives little attention compared to other fields of machine learning, like Natural Language Modeling with LLMs, Reinforcement Learning with RL from human feedback, or Computer Vision with Diffusion models used in image generation. However, at the time of writing, the latest improvements in Gemini (Google LLM) were about refining the computational graph of the attention mechanism. In my opinion, this example illustrates the importance of learning Graph Machine Learning, and this series of articles is my effort to highlight it.

A great part of what is going to be written in this series is inspired by a wonderful book on graph machine learning (perhaps the best you can find), Graph Representation Learning [1]. Other parts will come from papers or resources I read during my PhD.

References

  1. Hamilton, William L. Graph representation learning. Morgan & Claypool Publishers, 2020.
  2. Veličković, Petar, et al. “Deep graph infomax.” Proceedings of International Conference on Learning Representations, 2019.
  3. Kipf, Thomas N., and Max Welling. “Semi-supervised classification with graph convolutional networks.” Proceedings of International Conference on Learning Representations, 2017.
  4. Hamilton, Will, Zhitao Ying, and Jure Leskovec. “Inductive representation learning on large graphs.” Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017).

link.title: Mastering Graph ML: GNNs and the message-passing framework

entry.content:
Graph neural networks promise to unlock the full power of relational data — but what really happens inside a GNN layer, and why does permutation equivariance matter so much? If you’ve ever used graphs in ML but still treat GNNs as a black box, this is where that stops.

Graph neural networks (GNNs), as their name suggests, are algorithms that work with graphs. Since graphs are a non-linear data structure, these models or algorithms need to account for the specific properties that stem from how graphs are represented mathematically.

Permutation equivariant assumption

As we have already seen in the first article of this series, Introduction to Graph Data, graphs are represented mathematically with the adjacency and feature matrices. In both these matrices, rows represent either the features of a node or its neighbors. To illustrate some specificities that GNNs need to account for, we’ll look at the adjacency matrix of a graph, but the problem remains the same with the feature matrix.

In the adjacency matrix, rows represent the neighbors of a node, so the first row represents the neighbors of node n°1, the second row represents the neighbors of node n°2, and so on.

However, the problem with this representation is that there is no such thing as node n°1 or node n°2 in a graph. The node numbering in a graph is arbitrary, and the following three representations for the same graph are equally valid

Even though several adjacency matrices can be different and represent the same graph, since there is one underlying graph, you want your model to predict the same value for this graph, regardless of which adjacency matrix you choose to represent it. To illustrate a bit, let’s take the example of a fraud detection model on a graph where nodes represent persons and edges represent transactions between them. The model should predict the same node as fraudsters, no matter which node numbering you choose. A fraudster is a fraudster regardless of the fact that it is modeled as node n°1, node n°2, or node n°10 in your graph.

Now, let’s look at the difficulties of building a model that outputs a single prediction for the same graph that can be represented differently as input. This may seem counterintuitive, as other deep learning models typically output different predictions for different input matrices. Hopefully, GNNs do not need to output the same prediction for totally different matrices. The several matrices that represent the same graph are related by permutation, which means that for each adjacency matrix, it is possible to retrieve another adjacency matrix of the same graph with a permutation matrix

Another aspect of working with graphs is that, in some cases, you don’t just need to predict something for whole graphs but also for nodes or edges in a graph. So, GNNs need to be equivariant to these permutations of the adjacency matrix rows, which means that a permutation of the input matrix results in the same permutation being applied to the output. By contrast, a model that is invariant means that a permutation of the input matrix does not change the output. To conclude, GNNs are special algorithms since they are equivariant to the permutations of the adjacency matrix rows of their input graph.

Being equivariant to all the permutations of the adjacency matrix rows of their input graph is a strong constraint on the model, and some researchers (including me) are trying to relax this constraint. For example, by building a model that would be equivariant to some but not all permutations of the adjacency matrix rows of their input graph.

Now that we have introduced a bit about the specificities of GNNs, but also every model that works with adjacency or feature matrices to represent a graph, let’s dive deeper into how GNNs, via the message passing scheme, can build node representations that incorporate features and structural information while remaining equivariant to node permutation.

The message passing framework

The message passing scheme or framework is a way to add structural information to the feature information contained in the feature matrix. While it is relatively simple to understand, it has demonstrated very strong performance on various graph-related tasks, such as node/edge classification, node/edge regression, or graph classification/regression.

So, how does the message passing scheme work? It starts by aggregating all the feature information from a node's neighbors.

Then it passes the neighborhood aggregation result along with the previous node representation into a non-linear update function. Note that this function is an elementwise function, which means that the output vector of this function is a vector of the same size as the input vector, where the function is applied independently to every element of the input vector.

After that, the output of the update function is the new node representation.

Finally, you repeat this process for each node in the graph, and this completes one layer of message passing over your graph.

As you can have already guessed, this framework is quite modular because you can design several aggregation functions, but also different update functions depending on the task you need to solve. We’ll go through three of the most popular variants of this framework in the next section: Graph Convolution Networks (GCNs)[2], Graph Attention Networks (GATs)[3], and GraphSAGE[4].

GNNs architectures

Basic GNNs

Before diving deeper into the three most popular GNN architectures, let’s look at the most general architecture of the GNN framework. It is simply the mathematical representation of the message-passing scheme that we’ve seen before, where the aggregation operator is the sum operator.

At iteration k, the node representation of a node u of the previous iteration (k-1) is denoted as

In this most general framework, the representation at the previous iteration of the node we’re trying to update is treated differently from the representation of its neighbors at the previous iteration. Hence, we define two trainable matrices, which means that the value of their components will be adjusted during training, Wself for the previous node representation and Wneigh for the previous node’s neighbors representation, such as

As hinted by the superscript k on Wself and Wneigh are specific to an iteration of the message-passing scheme (or layer). Generally, due to oversmoothing, a problem that I’ll cover in the next article, GNNs do not have as many layers as other Deep Learning algorithms (between 2 and 5 layers at most).

As a simplification of the message passing approach, it is common to add self-loops to the input graph and to omit the explicit update step for each node. This means that the representation at the previous iteration of the node we’re trying to update is no longer treated differently from the representation of its neighbors at the previous iteration. It is equivalent to sharing parameters between Wself and Wneigh matrices.

This is mathematically equivalent to defining the following message-passing

Then, to simplify even further the notation in the definition of GNN architectures, we can define graph-level update equations. These equations contain the node representation update, not just for one node but for every node of the input graph.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs)[2]

One notable issue with the aggregation operators in the basic GNN approaches is that it does not depend on the number of neighbors one node might have. Therefore, it can be highly sensitive to node degrees, and as with node statistics, you can normalize the aggregation operation using a symmetric normalization such as

Then, GCNs[2] are GNNs with the symmetric-normalized aggregation as well as the self-loop update approach

Hence, its graph-level update equation is

Graph Attention Networks (GATs)[3]

Another popular approach in GNNs is GATs[3], which builds on the idea to assign an attention weight or importance to each neighbor of the node we want to update the representation of, and then use these weights to weigh the neighbor’s influence during the aggregation step.

This idea of assigning weights to a node’s neighbors is directly inspired by the famous paper that defined the Transformer architecture in the context of natural language processing[5]. You could also see LLMs as GNNs working on a complete graph (a graph where every node is connected), where nodes are words or tokens in the original text.

But, first things first, how can we assign an attention weight to a node’s neighbors? To do this, you could apply a feedforward neural network to the concatenation of the two node representations you want to compute the attention score of

The message-passing scheme then becomes

However, one problem with this attention score computation is that the sum of the attention scores for a particular node does not sum up to one, which can lead to numerical instabilities as the components of node representations grow larger and larger after each layer of the message-passing scheme. Therefore, as always, we need to normalize and, here more specifically, transform the attention score into a probability distribution. One way to do that is to use the softmax function

To understand how it works in the context of GNNs, let’s take an example of a graph with 3 nodes. We want to update the representation of node n°1. First, we apply the feedforward neural network

Then, we need to use the softmax function to get a probability distribution

Finally, we can use the attention score to weigh node representations of the previous iteration in the message-passing scheme

Hence, the normalized attention scores become

And the message-passing scheme is defined as

Like the transformer architecture, GATs[3] allow the use of multiple attention “heads”. These heads are independent attention mechanisms that stabilise the training process since the model does not depend on one attention mechanism, which could get stuck in a local optimum. It also allows the model to focus on different parts of the input at the same time using these different attention heads.

Therefore, the model now computes attention scores for each pair of nodes and each attention head. Hence, there is one update node representation for each attention head

The message passed during the message-passing scheme is then the concatenation of the update node representation for each attention head

GraphSAGE[4]

Another approach that, in theory, can generalize more naturally to unseen nodes is GraphSAGE[4]. Rather than assigning a unique embedding to each node, as previous algorithms do, it focuses on training a collection of aggregator functions. These functions are designed to combine feature information from the local neighborhoods of nodes, with each function responsible for aggregating data from varying hop distances. Then, during inference, the model leverages these trained aggregation functions to create embeddings for nodes it has never encountered before.

As described in the paper [4], let’s first outline the forward propagation, i.e., the embedding generation, which assumes the model has already been trained. We’ll see afterwards how the model is trained.

The algorithm of the forward propagation operates by progressively iterating through different hop distances (or levels of search depth). At each step, nodes gather information from their immediate neighbors, and with each subsequent iteration, they gradually accumulate insights from increasingly distant parts of the graph.

At each iteration k, a node v combines the representations of its immediate neighbors into a single vector.

Following this aggregation, GraphSAGE merges the node’s current representation with the aggregated neighborhood vector by concatenating them. The resulting vector is then passed through a fully connected layer with a nonlinear activation function.

To avoid any numerical instabilities, they normalize every node representation at each iteration k

Finally, the final representation output at depth K is the node embedding we’ll keep.

Another interesting idea from the GraphSAGE model is its use of neighborhood sampling. Instead of aggregating features from an entire neighborhood, it selects a fixed-size sample of neighbors through uniform sampling. This approach ensures that the computational cost for each batch remains consistent.

Now that we’ve seen how embeddings are generated at inference time with the GraphSAGE algorithm, let’s explain how the aggregation functions are trained in a fully unsupervised setting to generate meaningful node embeddings.

In the GraphSAGE framework, three candidate aggregation functions were used: mean aggregator, pooling aggregator, and LSTM aggregator.

First, the mean aggregator is almost equivalent to the convolution propagation rule we’ve seen in GCNs

A key difference between the mean aggregator in GraphSAGE and the convolutional aggregator in GCNs is that the mean aggregator skips the concatenation step. In contrast, the convolutional aggregator in GCNs combines the node’s previous layer representation with the aggregated neighborhood vector through concatenation.

Then, in the pooling aggregator approach, each neighbor’s vector is independently fed through a fully connected neural network. Following this transformation, an element-wise max-pooling operation is applied to aggregate information across the neighbor set.

In their ablation studies, the authors did not find a significant difference between max- and mean-pooling. So it seems that the two could be used interchangeably.

Lastly, a more advanced aggregator leverages the LSTM architecture, offering greater expressive power compared to the other aggregators. However, because LSTMs process inputs sequentially, they lack symmetry (i.e., they are not inherently permutation invariant), which is necessary for the overall model to maintain permutation equivariance. To address this, the authors modified LSTMs to handle unordered sets by applying them to a random permutation of the node’s neighbors.

The final part of the training process is to design a loss function to get gradients to tune the weight matrices in whichever aggregator function you choose. In GraphSAGE, the following loss is used in a fully unsupervised setting

The idea behind this equation is that this graph-based loss function encourages nearby nodes to have similar representations (left part), while enforcing that the representations of disparate nodes are highly distinct (right part). Let’s explain step by step.

First, let’s focus on the left part

z_u and z_v represent node embeddings of nodes u and v that co-occur on fixed-length random walks. Therefore, we want these embeddings to be quite similar. A way to measure the similarity between these two vectors is to multiply them and apply the sigmoid function σ. In this case, the higher the value, the more similar the two vectors are. Hence, minimizing (-1)log of that quantity enforces the two vectors to be similar. That’s why minimizing this part of the loss function during training enforces the model to produce similar embeddings for nearby nodes.

Then, the right part of the equation

Even though the notation seems more difficult, this part of the loss function follows the same idea as the other one. Let’s first explain Pn. The negative sampling distribution Pn allows us to draw nodes of the input graph that are highly disparate (i.e., they do not co-occur on fixed-length random walks). In that case, we want their embeddings to be distinct, hence we use the measure of similarity as before, with the difference being that instead of multiplying z_u and z_v together, we multiply (-1)z_u and z_v. In this setting, the higher the value, the more distinct the two embeddings will be. That’s why minimizing this part of the loss function during training enforces the model to produce distinct embeddings for highly disparate nodes. Finally, Q balances the importance between building similar embeddings for nearby nodes and building distinct embeddings for disparate nodes.

Training aggregator functions rather than individual embeddings allows GraphSAGE to serve as an inductive framework that efficiently utilizes node feature information to generate embeddings for nodes it has not seen during training.

Conclusion

So far, we’ve seen how the message-passing framework works in GNNs. It first aggregates the representation of a node’s neighbors and then passes this aggregation into a non-linear update function that outputs the updated node representation. As a general framework, message-passing GNNs have many variations, of which we have explained three of the most used: GCNs[2], GATs[3], and GraphSAGE[4].

What’s coming next? Even though message-passing GNNs are quite powerful in many applications, they do come with several disadvantages or weaknesses. We’ll cover them in the next article while explaining some of the tricks that can be used to tackle them.

entry.title: Mastering Graph ML: Node embeddings
entry.content:
Embeddings are crucial in machine learning models, as they provide a good way to represent complex data structures in compact vector representations. Graph data is no exception to this, and here’s how you build node embeddings.

What are node embeddings?

As in other domains of machine learning or representational learning, embeddings are representations of objects in a latent space that we choose, where geometric relations correspond to relationships between objects in the original space. Hence, node embeddings are representations of nodes in a latent space (usually as a vector of real numbers), where geometric relations correspond to relationships, such as edges, in the original graph.

For instance, let’s say we have the following graph, and we want to represent the three nodes u, v, and w with one number (1D embedding).

Since u and v are connected in the graph, their representation should be closer in the embedding space than with the representations of node w. For 1D embedding, this means that the distance between the numbers by which we choose to represent them should be less than the distance between the representations of node u and node w, as well as the representations of node v and node w.

The same idea holds when you increase the dimension of your embedding space. For example, if we choose to represent nodes with two real numbers, then the distance in R² between node representations should verify the same properties as with a 1-dimensional embedding space.

Again, the same property is true for higher-dimensional embeddings. Usually, node embeddings have a higher dimension since representing nodes with only two numbers does not account for the complexity of their relationship with other nodes in the original graph.

Note that node embeddings are different from node features, which we’ll get to in the next section on Deep Learning Methods. Node features are not used in these methods, and the node embeddings try to represent only the structural information of the graph for each node.

Encoder-decoder approaches

The first approach to building node embeddings is the encoder-decoder approach. As the name suggests, it involves an encoder that takes as input the adjacency matrix of the graph and outputs node embedding vectors. However, the encoder still needs a training task to optimize the node embeddings; this is where the decoder part is useful.

The decoder will take the node embeddings as input and will try to reconstruct graph statistics from them. The standard approach is to define a pairwise decoder that predicts the similarity score between pairs of nodes.

The similarity score matrix S is derived from the adjacency matrix A, but it might also be adjusted to include additional information. For instance, if u and v are neighbors in the graph, then S[u,v] = 1, but S[u,v] = 0.5 if they share a common neighbor even though they are not directly connected.

The goal is then to optimize the encoder and decoder to minimize the reconstruction loss so that

After the training phase, you can get rid of the decoder, and the node embeddings can be accessed through the encoder.

Matrix-factorization approaches

Another way of building node embeddings is by viewing this task as using matrix factorization to learn a low-dimensional approximation of the pairwise similarity matrix S.

I’m not particularly familiar with these methods, but I still wanted to highlight this interesting way of thinking about node embeddings. If you want to learn more about these approaches, you should check the most popular methods: graph factorization[7], GraRep[8], and HOPE[9].

Random walk approaches

The final way of building node embeddings that we’ll explore is using random walks. The idea with random walks embeddings is that two nodes have similar embeddings if they tend to co-occur on short random walks over the graph. One benefit of the random walk approaches is that they can be extended and modified by biasing or modifying the random walks. For instance, you could give higher probabilities of occurring in the random walk to the nodes you’ve already visited, or the other way around.

So, when you have node sequences from random walks, how can you build node embeddings from them? Random walks node embeddings algorithms use a similar architecture to the one used to get word embeddings using the word2vec skip-gram method[2], where the goal is to predict the words that will be in the context of a target word. Hence, I’ll start by explaining this method from natural language processing.

With words, you’ll use a sliding window that looks at the words before and after the target word to get the sequence of training samples. If you use a sliding window of size 5, you’ll build your training examples from the French simple sentence “Le chien est dans la maison” as follows.

After getting these training sequences, in the word2vec skip-gram model, both the input vector and the output are one-hot encoded word representations. This means that for every word in the dictionary, you create a vector with a one value and zeros everywhere else. The position in the vector where you put the one value is unique to every word, so you could have something like the first word of the dictionary has a one at position 1 and zeros everywhere else, and the second word of the dictionary has a one at position 2 and zeros everywhere else, and so on.

The word2vec skip-gram model[2] is then a neural network with one hidden layer and an input layer and an output layer of the same size corresponding to the size of the vocabulary, since the input and output vectors are one-hot encoded. In this model, after training, the weights of the model will represent all the word representations.

Now, how can we translate into getting node embeddings? First, we need to build a training dataset with node sequences that will have the same role as sentences in the word2vec skip-gram model[2]. Then, we’ll build training samples in the same way as before, with (target word, context word), but in the case of node embeddings, tuples (target node, context node) will be built using a sliding window on the node sequences.

The two most used methods to generate random walk embeddings, DeepWalk[4] and node2vec[5], differ in how they define the training node sequences. Based on the explanations in [6], let’s analyse both of them.

First, DeepWalk[4] uses random walks to generate several node sequences starting from each node in the graph. To generate these training node sequences, it starts from a node and uniformly samples the next node from the neighbors of the current node. This means that for a specific node, all neighbors have the same probability of being visited at the next step of the random walk.

Let’s take the same graph as before and start the node sequences from node 1.

All neighbors of node 1 (here, 3 and 4) will have the same probability of being visited at the next step of the random walk.

Then, let’s assume the random walk goes to node 3. Again, all neighbors of node 3 (here, 1, 2, 4, and 5) will have the same probability of being visited at the next step of the random walk.

This iteration continues until it reaches the desired random walk length.

Similarly, the node2vec algorithm also uses random walks to generate several node sequences starting from each node in the graph. The difference with node2vec[5] compared to DeepWalk[4] is that the algorithm generates node sequences using second-order walks that take into account both the current as well as the previous state.

Let’s see how it changes the node sequences that we build for our training dataset, and start with the same graph as before, from node 1.

At the first step, since the random walk did not visit any node at the previous step (since there is no previous step), the node neighbors' probabilities of getting visited remain the same as with DeepWalk[4].

Then, let’s assume the random walk goes to node 3. This is where node2vec[5] and DeepWalk[4] differ. node2vec[5] allows taking into account nodes that have been visited before, but also nodes that are not neighbors with nodes previously visited. To do so, we assign a weight 1/p to nodes that have been visited before and a weight 1/q to nodes that are not neighbors with nodes previously visited in the random walk.

The values p and q are chosen as hyperparameters of the model, and they influence how the random walks visit the graph.

First, choosing a low value for p (p<1) encourages the random walk to stay close to the starting node. On the contrary, setting a high value for p (p>1) encourages more exploration within the graph.

Then, q also influences how the random walks go through the graph. Setting a low value of q (q<1) encourages the model to visit nodes further away from the starting node, which corresponds to an approximation of a depth-first search in the graph. Conversely, choosing a high value of q (q>1) biases the random walks to visit nodes close to the node in the previous step, which corresponds to an approximation of a breadth-first search in the graph.

Drawbacks of traditional node embeddings

Even though traditional node embeddings are quite powerful tools to build a node representation that takes into account the structural information induced by the graph data structure, they are not perfect and come with some disadvantages.

First, these node embeddings can be quite computationally expensive and not well optimized. Indeed, these embedding methods do not share any parameters between nodes in the model or encoder, since they directly optimize a unique embedding vector for each node.

Also, they are inherently transductive, meaning that these methods can only generate embeddings for nodes that were present during the training phase, which can be harmful for some applications with regularly changing graphs, like social networks or molecules in a chemical reaction. Besides, and perhaps more importantly, these methods do not leverage node features but only the structural information.

That will motivate new methods to get node representations without these drawbacks. We’ll see about them in the next section on Deep Learning Methods.

Conclusion

This article concludes the section on Traditional approaches to machine learning on graphs. So far, we’ve seen how we can construct features or statistics from the structural information embedded in the graph data structure. However, these methods were not perfect and especially since they did not use the features or attributes that nodes or edges can have. Deep Learning methods on graphs are an attempt to leverage both structural information from the graph and the feature information.

What’s coming next? The next article will start the section about Deep Learning Methods on graphs. Especially, it will present the message passing mechanism, which is at the heart of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), but also several tricks that can be used to improve them.

link.title: Mastering Graph ML: Graph Spectral Clustering

entry.content:
Sometimes, deep learning is not required, and mathematics is enough. Let’s break down how spectral analysis and graph Laplacians reveal meaningful communities in graphs.

Introduction to graph clustering

Graph clustering (or community detection) is the task of detecting meaningful groups or clusters of nodes within a graph. To define optimal clusters, we first need to define a metric that measures how well-defined a cluster is. For that, we use the notion of a cut in a graph. It is simply the count of how many edges cross the boundary between the partitions of nodes.

Let’s illustrate this definition with the following graph and partitions

First, we need to count the number of outgoing edges of the partition A₁

Then we iterate this operation for all the partitions of nodes.

Finally, we can compute the cut of the partitions of nodes with the counts that we have measured before

To my knowledge, the graph cut is only used to compare node partitions between them; the lower the value the better, but there is no absolute value that would mean the node partition studied is optimal.

However, the graph cut is biased towards building partitions of nodes with degree 1. For instance, if you want to detect clusters in the following graph

A natural partition of the nodes would be

However, if you calculate it, its graph cut would be higher than the following partition of nodes

This partition is better according to the graph cut metrics, but you can easily see that this partition makes less sense than the previous one. Therefore, we need to modify the metric to account for the number of nodes in the different clusters. To tackle this, we use the normalisation of the graph cut, the graph RatioCut, in which we divide the number of outgoing edges of each cluster by its number of nodes:

Now that we have introduced how we can measure the performance of a clustering assignment, we’ll need to introduce some mathematical concepts that’ll help you understand the algorithm of graph spectral clustering.

Introduction to spectral analysis

To analyze the graph’s structure through the adjacency matrix, we’ll use a powerful mathematical tool from linear algebra: spectral analysis, which focuses on eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Eigenvalues/vectors are instrumental to understanding electrical circuits, mechanical systems, quantum physics and even Google’s PageRank algorithm.

Also, to understand these concepts better, it is important to know that eigen is a German word meaning own or typical. Hence, an eigenvector can also be called a characteristic vector, and an eigenvalue a characteristic value of a matrix.

Let’s start with a formal definition: for a square matrix A, an eigenvector is a non-zero vector that satisfies the equation

This equation means that when the matrix A acts on the eigenvector, it only scales it by a factor of λ, without changing its direction. This property is important because it identifies inherent directions or patterns in the data, where the scaling factor λ quantifies the importance or strength of that pattern.

Let’s use an example from physics to illustrate this a bit. Imagine a guitar string that vibrates when plucked. The string’s vibration patterns are determined by its physical properties. Each vibration mode corresponds to a specific pattern of movement along the string. For example:

  • The first mode (fundamental frequency) is when the entire string moves up and down uniformly.
  • The second mode is when the string bends into two segments, with a point of no movement in the middle.
  • Higher modes involve increasingly more complex patterns.

These modes are the eigenvectors of the system because they describe the directions in which the string naturally vibrates. Each of these modes vibrates at a specific frequency, which depends on the string’s tension, length, and mass. These frequencies are the eigenvalues of the system associated with an eigenvector (they determine the pitch of the sound produced by the string).

I hope that this part was clear enough for you to understand that eigenvectors and eigenvalues are mathematical tools that allow us to find patterns in the data. I didn’t specify how we can find and calculate them because I just wanted to introduce their motivations, but if you’re interested, you should check [2], [3], and [4].

Graph spectral clustering

Before finally getting to the graph spectral clustering algorithm, I need to introduce the graph Laplacian. This matrix is particularly relevant for graph signal processing as its eigenvectors and eigenvalues will be the center of the spectral analysis of graph signals. The graph Laplacian is defined as

The graph Laplacian measures how different a node is from its neighbors. If all neighbors of a node have similar signal values, the Laplacian value will be small, and if there is a large difference between a node and its neighbors, the Laplacian value will be large.

It also plays a central role in the graph signal processing framework, serving as the graph’s equivalent of the Laplacian operator in classical signal processing, which is fundamental for tasks like filtering, smoothing, and spectral analysis.

Why are we studying the graph Laplacian spectrum? The reason for that is that the graph Laplacian spectrum has several interesting properties about the graph :

  • The smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian is λ₁​=0, and its eigenvector is a constant vector 1 (all ones). This corresponds to the trivial mode where there is no variation across the graph.
  • The second smallest eigenvalue λ₂, called the algebraic connectivity, measures how well the graph is connected. A larger λ₂ indicates a more connected graph, while λ₂=0 indicates the graph is disconnected.
  • Also, the geometric multiplicity of the 0 eigenvalue (number of independent eigenvectors for which 0 is an eigenvalue) of the Laplacian L corresponds the the number of connected components in the graph.

Finally, the last and most important property (for this article) of this spectrum is: the second-smallest eigenvector of the graph Laplacian is a continuous approximation to the discrete vector that gives an optimal cluster assignment for 2 clusters (with respect to the RatioCut). So what does that mean?

First, the second-smallest eigenvector refers to the eigenvector of the second-smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian.

After that, a continuous approximation to the discrete vector that gives an optimal cluster assignment for 2 clusters (with respect to the RatioCut) means that if the vector that assigns a node to either cluster 0 or cluster 1 with an optimal cluster assignment (the lowest RatioCut value) is as such

Then, the second-smallest eigenvector of the graph Laplacian would look something like this

By discretizing the values (if value > 0 then 1 else 0), you would get the previous vector that assigns a node to either cluster 0 or cluster 1 with an optimal cluster assignment.

Generalized graph spectral clustering

The problem with the former property is that this result is only good for getting 2 clusters, but what happens when you want to get more clusters than that?

You can generalize the idea of graph spectral clustering to any arbitrary number of clusters (it still has to be less than the number of nodes). Here are the steps of the algorithm :

  1. Find the K smallest eigenvectors of L (excluding the smallest since it is constant over nodes, so it does not provide much information)
  2. Form the matrix U with the eigenvectors of step 1
  3. Represent each node by its corresponding row in the matrix U
  4. Run K-means clustering on the embeddings from step 3

Let’s illustrate this with an example and take a graph with 10 nodes, in which we want to extract 3 clusters

import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

G = nx.erdos_renyi_graph(10, 0.3, seed=42)  # Random graph with 10 nodes
nx.draw(G, with_labels=True, node_color='skyblue', node_size=700)
plt.title("Original Graph")
plt.show()

Then we calculate its adjacency matrix A as explained in my previous article, and its degree matrix D by counting the number of neighbors for each node.

A = nx.adjacency_matrix(G).todense()
D = np.diag(np.sum(A, axis=1))

Then, we have everything we need to compute the graph Laplacian with the formula: L = D - A.

L = D - A
# Or you can directly compute it from the networkx module
L = nx.laplacian_matrix(G).toarray()

After that, we need to get the K=3 smallest eigenvectors of L. For that, I’ll use the scipy built-in module that computes all the eigenvalues of a matrix and its associated eigenvectors.

from scipy.linalg import eigh

eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eigh(L)

You can now extract the three smallest eigenvectors of L to get the matrix U that will represent the nodes in the graph.

K = 3  # Number of clusters
U = eigenvectors[:, 1:K+1]  # Exclude the smallest eigenvector (1st column)

At that moment, you have a 3-dimensional vector representing each node by taking the rows of the U matrix. So the first row represents node n°1, the second row represents node n°2 and so and so on. You can use these representations or embeddings to do traditional clustering using algorithms such as K-means or KNNs. For this example, we’ll use K-means with the scikit-learn Python module.

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=K, random_state=0)
labels = kmeans.fit_predict(U)

Finally, you only need to plot the results to see how the generalized spectral algorithm has clustered the nodes in the original graph.

from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D 

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 6))

# Plot 3D node embeddings
ax = plt.subplot(1, 2, 1, projection='3d')  
sc = ax.scatter(U[:, 0], U[:, 1], U[:, 2], 
                c=labels, cmap='viridis', s=100)
ax.set_title("Node Embeddings (3D)")
ax.set_xlabel("Eigenvector 1")
ax.set_ylabel("Eigenvector 2")
ax.set_zlabel("Eigenvector 3")
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="Cluster Labels") 

# Plot graph with cluster coloring
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
pos = nx.spring_layout(G, seed=42) 
nx.draw(G, pos, with_labels=True, node_color=labels, cmap='viridis', node_size=700)
plt.title("Graph with Clusters")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Conclusion

To conclude, after reading this article, you should be able to extract clusters from a graph without deep learning algorithms and to evaluate them using Cut and RatioCut measures. I hope the practical example with code was helpful to understand how the spectral analysis for cluster optimization is made and how it works better than with just the theoretical explanation.

What’s coming next? The next article of the Traditional Approaches section will present node embeddings. Especially, why they are useful, and how relationships in the original graph correspond to geometric relations in the latent space of these node representations.
