link.title: Mastering Graph ML: Node, Edge, and Graph Statistics

entry.content:
Unlock the foundational concepts of Graph Machine Learning by exploring traditional techniques used to extract graph insights from node, edge, and graph-level statistics, as well as advanced concepts like graph kernels and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.

Before delving deeper into understanding graph machine learning and graph neural networks (GNNs), in my opinion, it is necessary to understand the traditional approaches used in machine learning with graph data, which paved the way for the graph machine learning models we use today.

Traditional approaches in graph ML

Traditional approaches to machine learning using graph data begin by extracting some statistics or features, based on heuristic functions or domain knowledge, and then use these features/statistics as input to a standard machine learning model.

As graphs involve two types of objects, namely nodes and edges, there are often three categories of features that are usually used in traditional approaches: node statistics, edge statistics, and graph statistics. I’ll try to make sense to you of the most popular ones in each category in this article.

Node statistics

At the node level, the four main statistics used in traditional methods in machine learning using graph data are: node degree, eigenvector centrality, betweenness centrality, and local clustering coefficient.

The degree of a node is the number of neighbors one node has. Recall that at this stage, we have already represented the graph with the adjacency and features matrices. Therefore, how can we compute the node degree from these matrices? It is computed by summing over the rows of the adjacency matrix :

Remember how we built the adjacency matrix, we first filled row n°1 and put a 1 in the position corresponding to node n°1's neighbors, then we did the same for every other node in the graph.

Hence, summing over the rows in an undirected and unweighted graph gives the number of neighbors. On the contrary, in a directed graph, the scientific literature makes a distinction between the in-degree, meaning the degree corresponding to incoming edges, and the out-degree, meaning the degree regarding outgoing edges.

The eigenvector centrality measures the importance of a node in a network by considering not just the number of its connections, but also the importance of the nodes it is connected to. Unlike other centrality measures like the node degree, the eigenvector centrality doesn’t just look at the number of connections a node has — it also considers how important the connected nodes are. In other words, being connected to influential nodes increases your influence. Think of it like this: In a social network, being friends with a few highly popular people (like celebrities) might make you more “central” than being friends with a large number of less influential people.

To calculate eigenvector centrality, we use a mathematical concept called an eigenvector. It is a special kind of vector used in linear algebra. When you multiply a matrix by an eigenvector, the result is the same eigenvector scaled by a constant (called the eigenvalue).
Mathematically, this looks like:

In simple terms, the eigenvector tells us how influence or importance is distributed across the nodes in the network.

To compute the eigenvector centrality, we start with an initial guess for the scores (i.e., all nodes have equal scores). Then, we repeatedly update each node’s score to be proportional to the sum of the scores of its neighbors. This process continues until the scores stabilize, which corresponds to finding the eigenvector of the adjacency matrix.

The eigenvector centrality is quite a powerful tool, as PageRank, the algorithm that ranks pages in the Google search engine, is a variant of the eigenvector centrality.

On the other hand, betweenness centrality measures how important a node is in terms of connecting other nodes in the network. Specifically, it quantifies how often a node lies on the shortest paths (or geodesics for geometrical nerds) between pairs of other nodes. In simple terms, a node with high betweenness centrality acts like a “bridge” in the network, helping to connect different parts of the graph. It’s particularly useful for identifying nodes that control the flow of information or resources in a network.

Now that you got that, the idea behind betweenness centrality is to count how many of the shortest paths between all pairs of nodes pass through a given node. Let’s see how it is computed. First, for every pair of nodes in the network, find all the shortest paths between them. Then, for each node, count how many of these shortest paths pass through it. If a node lies on many shortest paths, it has a high betweenness score.

It can be especially useful in transportation networks to find critical roads, airports, or train stations that connect regions.

Finally, the local clustering coefficient measures how tightly connected the neighbors of a node are or how close the neighborhood of a node is compared to a complete graph (a graph where all nodes are connected). If you think of a social network, the clustering coefficient measures how many of your friends are also friends with each other.

How can you compare one node neighborhood to a complete graph? Since having a high clustering coefficient would mean that one node's neighbors are connected to other neighbors of the same node, one could suggest counting the number of edges between neighboring nodes. It would be a start, but this measure would be biased towards nodes with a high degree. Indeed, a node with 3 neighbors connected together only has 3 edges between neighboring nodes will have a lower clustering coefficient than a node with 50 neighbors and 5 edges between them. Hence, we need to normalize by the number of possible edges between neighboring nodes. For that, we can take the number of possible pairs of nodes in a node neighborhood. The local clustering coefficient is therefore defined as

The clustering coefficient is important because it tells us about the local density of the graph. For instance, in social networks, it can measure how tightly-knit groups or communities are, and in biological networks, it can help identify clusters of highly interacting entities, like proteins or genes.

Edge statistics

Now that we’ve seen several ways to get statistics on nodes, it might be time to also get statistics on what connects them. The goal with edge statistics is to design features that capture the structure of edges in the graph to use in a traditional machine learning algorithm to predict new edges based on existing ones.

At the edge-level, to my knowledge, the three main edge statistics are: distance-based features, local, and global neighborhood overlap measures.

The most basic method to get edge-level statistics is to use distance-based features, which calculate the shortest path between two nodes. You can compute the shortest path between two nodes using a well-known algorithm like Dijkstra [2], A* [3], Breadth-First Search [4], or any other shortest-path finder algorithm. I won’t cover them in this series, but feel free to learn about them in the resources I’ve put in the references.

Sometimes, using only distance-based features is not enough, and we want to quantify the relationship between a pair of nodes. This is where statistical measures of neighborhood overlap are useful. They can be divided into two categories: local for pairs of nodes that have a two-hop distance between them, and global, which attempt to take relationships beyond the local node neighborhood into account.

The simplest neighborhood overlap counts the number of neighbors that two nodes share

However, this formula is biased towards nodes with a degree. Indeed, let’s say we want to get the statistics on two pairs of nodes (node n°1, node n°2) and (node n°2, node n°3). If node n°1 has 25 neighbors, of which 3 are also connected to node n°2, and node n°3 has 2 neighbors, all of them common with node n°2. The statistics will be higher for the pair (node n°1, node n°2), even though, regarding their whole neighborhoods, node n°3 seems to be more related to node n°2. Therefore, it can be useful to use normalization on this measure

One problem with local neighborhood overlap measures is that they are useless with nodes that do not have a two-hop distance between them. Therefore, we need features that take the relationship beyond the local node neighborhood into account. Global neighborhood overlap measures attempt to do so.

Before throwing at you the Katz index formula (one of the most popular global neighborhood overlap measures), I need to discuss the interesting properties of the powers of the adjacency matrix. Here, I refer to the power of a matrix as the multiplication by itself and not some kind of superpower. You can see the nth power of the adjacency matrix as the matrix that counts the number of paths of length n between a pair of nodes.

So let’s start with the adjacency matrix A. A path of length 1 is just an edge, so the adjacency matrix can be interpreted as a matrix that counts the number of paths of length 1 (edges) between nodes.

Then, what happens when we multiply A by itself? Then, you get the matrix that counts the number of all paths of length 2 between nodes. Feel free to prove it mathematically; it’s not that hard [5], but I won’t do it here; I’ll just show an illustration.

The same happens if you multiply one more time A² by A to get A³.

I’ll stop here because I think you got it. But what do the powers of the adjacency matrix have to do with the Katz index? Well, the Katz index counts the number of paths of all lengths between a pair of nodes by using the powers of the adjacency matrix. It also weights them to give lower importance to paths of high length.

As such, we’re able to compute meaningful statistics even between nodes that do not have a two-hop distance between them. Since the sum goes to infinity, we will find a path between any two nodes, and the longer this path, the lower the Katz index will be because of the constant β.

Graph statistics

Graph kernel methods are a class of techniques in machine learning used to compare and analyze graphs. A graph kernel is a function that computes the similarity between two graphs.

The key idea in graph kernels is to define a feature vector ϕ(G) that can differentiate between two different graphs.

These high-dimensional feature vectors can then be used to represent entire graphs rather than individual nodes or edges and to compute the graph kernel (the measure of similarity between graphs).

It might seem a bit abstract for now, but let’s use an example to illustrate what does graph kernel means. The simplest approach to defining a graph-level feature is just to aggregate node-level statistics, which is known as bag-of-nodes. For instance, you could just choose to aggregate node degrees.

However, bag-of-nodes is entirely based upon local node-level information and therefore can miss important global properties in the graph.

That’s why iterative neighborhood aggregation approaches want to extract node-level features that contain more information than just their local ego graph, as in bag-of-nodes methods, and then to aggregate these richer features into a graph-level representation.

The most used approach is to use features from the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test. It is extremely important because one of the most influential graph ML papers [6] has demonstrated that GNNs within the MPNN framework are at best as powerful as this test to distinguish between two graphs. But I’ll cover that in later articles.

So, how does the WL test work? It works in several steps: one initialisation step, a repeated process of two steps, and a final step to retrieve the feature vector. Then, you just need to compare the feature vectors: if they are equal, then, according to the test, the two graphs are the same.

Let’s start with the following two graphs

First, you assign initial colors to the nodes

Then, your aggregate neighboring colors

After that, you hash the aggregated colors. Here, hashing just means assigning a unique new value to every unique aggregation of neighboring colors of the previous step.

You can then repeat the two previous steps until you are satisfied with the aggregation depth.

Finally, you count the frequency of hash values during the test, and you get the feature vector that represents your graph.

By using the aggregation mechanism, the WL test captures both local and global structural information. However, it still has some limitations with simple peculiar graphs. For instance, the test cannot differentiate between these two graphs

In this case, the WL test fails because the aggregation and hashing steps are unable to detect if two nodes share a neighbor.

Another valid and powerful strategy for defining features over graphs is to simply count the occurrence of different small subgraph structures, usually called graphlets in this context.

For instance, let’s say we want to study these graphlets

First, we’ll look for the graphlet g1 in the graph we want to study, and we’ll find only one

Then, we do the same for g2, g3, and g4.

Finally, we get the feature vector by aggregating the frequencies in the graph of each graphlet.

An alternative to enumerating all possible graphlets, which can be quite expensive computationally speaking, is to use path-based methods. In these approaches, we simply examine the different kinds of paths that occur in the graph.

Conclusion

That’s it for today! I hope the article didn’t feel like a shopping list where I presented several statistics with no context or connections between them. Nonetheless, I truly believe that getting to know traditional approaches to machine learning using graph data is key to understanding graph neural networks. The most important thing to take away from this article is the aggregation and update (with the hashing function) mechanisms of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, as GNNs can be thought of as a continuous analog of these mechanisms.

What’s coming next? The next article of the Traditional Approaches part will discuss graph spectral clustering. It will introduce Fourier analysis on a graph and its spectral properties. Especially, how one can use the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian to learn node clusters.

entry.title: Mastering Graph ML: Introduction to Graph Data

link.title: Mastering Graph ML: Introduction to Graph Data

entry.content:
Ever wondered how social networks recommend friends or how scientists predict molecular properties? The answer lies in graphs — a way to represent data that captures relationships and patterns.

While traditional tabular data falls short in capturing connections, graphs excel by modeling the structure of complex systems. In this series of articles, we’ll break down the basics of graph data and how machine learning leverages it to solve real-world problems. Whether you’re a beginner or just curious, this is your gateway to understanding graph-powered insights.

Introduction to Graph Data

The first step to understanding Graph Machine Learning is to understand graphs. I’ll try to introduce this data structure and how it can be represented. It will be an introduction, and I encourage you to learn more about the mathematics of graph theory.

What is Graph-structured Data?

Graphs are non-linear data structures composed of nodes and edges. Let’s break it down. Nodes are the basic units of a graph, and are connected by edges. To illustrate what I’m saying, I’ll give you an example. Let’s say you have a social network consisting of four people.

Then, you’ll link them if they ever exchanged a message on the social network.

Congrats! You have successfully built your first graph. The users of the social network are the nodes, and the links you made between them are edges.

Now, why are graphs considered non-linear data structures, and what are non-linear data structures? To understand non-linear data structures, we must introduce linear data structures. Linear data structures are a type of data structure in computer science where data elements are arranged sequentially or linearly [2].

What does this mean for graphs? Nodes and edges are not arranged sequentially or linearly. Instead, they are arranged in sets, which is why graphs are considered non-linear data structures. You can think of sets as lists where there is no fixed index, a bit like a bag of balls where there is no ordering or numbering since the balls are all freely rolling in the bag. I hope you get the idea, but you must take home that there is no fixed numbering of nodes in a graph: no particular node is more relevant than the others to be labeled as node n°1 or node n°2 or any index you choose. Choosing indices for nodes or edges in the graph is arbitrary.

Why and When to Represent Data as Graphs?

As you may have already understood, graphs model relationships (edges) between objects (or nodes). They are quite powerful in problems where one might want to encode links within the data. Networks are a great example of graph applications, but you could also use graphs for molecules, where atoms are linked by covalent bonds.

Almost every data or problem can be modeled as a graph. Images can be graphs where nodes are pixels, and they share an edge if they are adjacent in the image. Text can be represented as graphs where nodes are words, and they share an edge if they have a semantic link between them. However, the problem is that a graph representation may not be optimal for every type of problem because sometimes representing a linear data structure like an image or a text as a non-linear data structure might come with more problems than solutions. So, you’ll need to be careful when representing your data as a graph that it is indeed the right data structure to use.

How can we Mathematically Represent a Graph?

Formally, a graph is defined by a set of nodes denoted by V and a set of edges E between these nodes.

However, in order to make calculations and especially machine learning on graphs, we need to make a numerical representation of a graph. This is where the adjacency matrix is useful. An adjacency matrix is a matrix where each row and column corresponds to a node, and the entries indicate whether a direct edge exists between the nodes. Let’s see how we can build this matrix.

As you can see in the images below, we start with the first row that will represent node n°1, and we then look at its neighbors.

In the example, node n°1 only has one neighbor node n°2, so we’ll put a 1 in position 2 and 0 everywhere else in the first row.

We then start the same process for all the nodes in the graph to fill the 3 remaining rows. For node n°2, we get

Then node n°3

Finally, node n°4

You may have already noticed, but the ordering we used between the nodes was arbitrary. Indeed, the same graph can be represented by different adjacency matrices depending on which node is node n°1, which node is node n°2, and so on.

We say that the different adjacency matrices of the same graph are related by permutations (rearrangements of rows and columns that correspond to reordering the nodes of the graph). Note that this property is extremely important, especially when designing models that work on graphs. Since the same graph can be represented by different adjacency matrices, a good model should return the same prediction when these different adjacency matrices are used as input. I’ll cover more on this later in the series when I introduce Graph Neural Networks and the message passing framework.

How can We Additionally Encode the Graph Information?

Now that we have mathematically represented graph structures, i.e., the connections between the nodes, we also need to represent the information about each node.

The node features represent this information. They are the numerical representations of the characteristics of each node. For instance, in social networks, the features of a node can be the verification status (whether or not a user has a verified account), age, and time spent on the network per day for the person that is represented by the node. For a molecular graph, it can be the atomic number, atomic mass, number of isotopes, and number of valence electrons.

A way to conveniently imagine feature information is by assigning a vector (a list of numbers) to each node in the graph.

Then, to aggregate all this information into a single object, you can use a matrix by stacking all the feature vectors for each node. This matrix is the feature matrix, and we’ll note it as X.

Two important remarks about this feature matrix. As you might have already noticed, this matrix also depends on the ordering of the nodes, which is arbitrary. Therefore, several feature matrices can represent the information of the same graph. These matrices, as adjacency matrices, are related by permutations. Also, the number of features you use (the size of the vector for each node) is totally up to the problem you’re solving and its design. Hence, the feature matrix size may change depending on what information you decide to keep in your graph.

Are There Other Types of Graphs?

Until now, I have focused on undirected graphs, but many other types of graphs exist, and models have been designed to perform learning on them. I’ll try to present the most popular ones now.

First, let’s talk about weighted, directed, and bipartite graphs, which are the closest to the undirected graphs we have presented so far.

A weighted graph is merely a graph where edges have been assigned weights. For example, a road network graph that uses cities as nodes and routes between them as edges might represent the fact that different routes don’t have the same length or travel time.

A directed graph is simply a graph where edges are directed, meaning that an edge from node 1 to node 2 is not the same as an edge from node 2 to node 1. Indeed, sometimes it can be useful to model the fact that a relationship between two nodes can be unilateral. If you think of a social network graph, being a follower or being followed by someone should not always be treated the same way.

A bipartite graph is a graph (undirected or directed and/or weighted) where the nodes can be divided into two separate categories such that all edges connect nodes present in one set to nodes in another set. For instance, in recommender systems, we could use graphs where users and items are represented as nodes, and there is an edge between the nodes if the user has purchased a particular item.

Other types of graphs change the structure of the graph. We’ll see only multidimensional graphs and hypergraphs, but many others can be used depending on your problem.

A multidimensional graph is a graph where two nodes can be related by more than one edge. Let’s take again a transportation network where cities are represented as nodes and routes between them as edges. Some cities can be connected by plane, train, and car. These connections should not be modeled the same way since their travel time and/or distance vary greatly depending on the mode of transport.

A hypergraph is a graph where one edge can connect more than two nodes. It can be useful when trying to model social network groups as a graph. The users are represented as nodes, and the groups are hyperedges (edges that connect several nodes) connecting several users.

The way to represent these hypergraphs is to use an adjacency matrix where rows represent nodes and columns represent hyperedges. In the example above, since the first column represents group A, nodes n°2, n°3, and n°4 (Julie, Louis, and Léa) are connected by this hyperedge; we put a 1 in positions 2, 3, and 4 in the column and 0 elsewhere.

Graph Machine Learning

Hopefully, now you should have understood the gist of how graph data works. You can already do a lot of analysis by just representing some data as graphs, and you should dive deeper into the mathematics of graph theory if you want to extract more from graph data without machine learning. But now it’s time to see what machine learning and graphs can accomplish when put together!

What can we do when combining graph data and machine learning together?

Since graph data differs a lot from traditional data, graph machine learning comes with its own set of tasks. I’ll try to emphasize the most popular ones, but there are a lot of them, and you should check if there is one that fits your problem.

One particularity of graph machine learning is that its tasks can be divided into 3 categories namely node-related tasks, where you want to predict a target for each node in a graph, edge-related tasks, where (you already guessed it …) you want to predict a target for each edge in a graph, and graph-related tasks, where you try to infer a target from whole graphs.

To my knowledge, the 7 most popular graph machine learning tasks are: node classification and regression, edge prediction, community detection, graph classification, graph regression, and graph clustering.

Node classification is a task where a model predicts a label for each node in the graph. A classic example would be fraud detection, where in a network of transactions (nodes as users and edges as transactions between them), you aim to predict which users are fraudsters.

Node regression

Edge prediction (or link prediction) aims to predict missing or future connections between nodes.

Community detection tries to find groups of nodes in a graph. You can see this task as a clustering problem within a graph. It can be particularly interesting for online targeting when a company tries to target people who are similar to the ones they already know to like their products.

Now I’ll focus on graph-related tasks where the models make predictions on whole graphs rather than on nodes or edges.

First, graph classification is quite straightforward. We ask the model to label different graphs. It is especially useful for biomedical applications. For instance, PROTEINS[5], a well-known dataset, represents proteins as graphs, and the goal is to classify them as enzymes or non-enzymes.

Graph regression is similar to other types of regression, but it works on graphs. Hence, the goal is to assign a scalar value (a number, basically) to a graph. Again, it is useful in biomedical applications when one might want to predict the toxicity as a number of a molecule that is represented as a graph.

Graph clustering is also similar to other types of clustering algorithms, but unlike community detection, it works on whole graphs. It can be useful when trying to find similar molecules that could interact well with each other.

Why Graph Machine Learning and not just traditional Deep Learning on graphs?

All of the tasks presented before are solved under consideration of both the adjacency and feature matrix. You could rightly wonder why we are trying to propose and build new methods specifically for graphs, whereas traditional machine learning and deep learning methods work well with matrices and could use the adjacency and feature matrix as inputs.

One problem with this idea is that traditional machine learning and deep learning methods have the identically and independently distributed assumption on data. What does that mean? As simply explained in [4], identically distributed means that every datapoint comes from the same distribution, i.e., if you take any large enough sample of your data, the mean and the variance should be the same.

For example, if you want to detect fraud in transaction networks (modeled as a graph or not), it means that the samples of the first 1000 transactions or the last 1000 transactions should approximately have the same mean and variance amount (or any sample of 1000 transactions). Note that the number 1000 transactions is arbitrary; I just wanted to show that this property arises with “large enough” samples. The identically distributed assumption stands with graph data since it has nothing to do with the structure of the graph, but rather the node features.

However, the independently distributed assumption does not hold when using graph data. Indeed, independently distributed means that there is no influence between datapoints, i.e., the outcome of one datapoint provides no information on the outcome of another datapoint.

For instance, if you want to predict the price of houses based on different features like surface, number of rooms, location … This assumption means that the prices of one house will not influence the price of other houses; it will only depend on the features of these houses. When using graph data, we are instead modeling an interconnected set of nodes and edges where we want the features of one node’s neighbors to influence the node prediction. Therefore, the independently distributed assumption of traditional machine learning and deep learning methods does not hold, and we need specific models to deal with graphs.

How can we account for graphs in machine learning?

When developing models, the graph machine learning community has come to exploit 3 main ideas to account for the specific type of data that is graphs: homophily, heterophily, and structural equivalence.

First, homophily is the tendency for nodes to share the same label as their neighbors. In the case of node classification, in a homophilic graph, nodes will tend to have the same target class as their neighbors.

Then, heterophily is the opposite. It’s the tendency for nodes to be preferentially connected to nodes with different labels. In the case of node classification, in a heterophilic graph, nodes will tend to have a different target class compared to those of their neighbors.

Finally, structural equivalence is the idea that nodes with similar local neighborhood structures will have similar labels. For instance, in node classification, that can mean that nodes with the same label can have the same degree (number of neighbors) or any measure on the neighborhood structure.

We’ll see in the article covering Graph Neural Networks how models attempt to leverage these three ideas to obtain good performances on graph machine learning tasks.

Conclusion

So far, we have focused on what graph data is and when it can be used, but also how we can represent it mathematically to use it with machine learning models. Without getting into the details of implementation, we have also seen the most popular tasks in graph machine learning and why it differs from traditional machine learning. I hope this gives you a solid and understandable introduction to graph machine learning while sparking your curiosity to discover more!

What’s coming next? The next article will start the Traditional Approaches part and will discuss node, edge, and graph statistics: How they are computed and how they can be useful to build good machine learning algorithms on graphs.

In my opinion, this example illustrates the importance of learning Graph Machine Learning, and this series of articles is my effort to highlight it.

A great part of what is going to be written in this series is inspired by a wonderful book on graph machine learning (perhaps the best you can find), Graph Representation Learning [1]. Other parts will come from papers or resources I read during my PhD.

This is how a post with tabs looks like. Note that the tabs could be used for different purposes, not only for code.

{% tabs group-name %}

Content 1

{% endtab %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-2 %}

Content 2

{% endtab %}

{% endtabs %}
